e-612.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
e-612.problem: Find $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \langle 6t^5+2t, \sec^2 t\rangle.$
e-612.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

e-613.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-615.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
e-615.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
e-615.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$

$$

$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

If F′(t)=⟨csc2⁡t,cos⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨−cot⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨−cot⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨cot⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨tan⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨csc2⁡t,cos⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨csc2⁡t,cos⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫csc2⁡tdt,∫cos⁡tdt⟩=⟨−cot⁡t+c1,sin⁡t+c2⟩=⟨−cot⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨−cot⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨e2t+5,cos⁡(t+1)⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨et2+5,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+C
b
⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+C
d
⟨e2t2,−cos⁡(t+1)⟩+C
e
⟨e2t5t,cos⁡(t+1)⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ∫(e^{2t}+5) dt = e^{2t}/2+5t and ∫cos(t+1) dt = sin(t+1). Thus option c has the required derivative.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{e}^{2t}+5,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{2t}+5,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int ({e}^{2t}+5)\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨e2t+5,cos⁡(t+1)⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨et2+5,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+C
b
⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+C
d
⟨e2t2,−cos⁡(t+1)⟩+C
e
⟨e2t5t,cos⁡(t+1)⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨e2t+5,sin⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨e2t+5,cos⁡(t+1)⟩dt=⟨∫(e2t+5)dt,∫cos⁡(t+1)dt⟩=⟨e2t2+5t+c1,sin⁡(t+1)+c2⟩=⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨e2t2+5t,sin⁡(t+1)⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: Option c differentiates to ⟨e^{2t}+5, cos(t+1)⟩ and matches the worked solution's final result. The initial sin(t) integrand in that solution is a typo. Option b differentiates to cos(t) in its second component, so it is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{e}^{2t}+5,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{2t}+5,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int ({e}^{2t}+5)\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+5t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

If F′(t)=⟨4t3−1,2et⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t4−t,e2t⟩+C
b
⟨4t2−t,2e2t⟩+C
c
⟨t4−t,2et⟩+C
d
⟨t3−1,2et⟩+C
e
⟨3t4−2t,12e2t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating each component gives ∫(4t³−1) dt = t⁴−t and ∫2eᵗ dt = 2eᵗ. Adding a constant vector yields option c.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨4{t}^{3}-1,\,2{e}^{t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨4{t}^{3}-1,\,2{e}^{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (4{t}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}t,2\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}-t+{c}_{1},\,2{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}-t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}-t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

before.html:
Question 4
?

If F′(t)=⟨4t3+2,t4⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t2−4t,t8⟩+C
b
⟨t4+2t,t28⟩+C
c
⟨2t4+2,t8⟩+C
d
⟨t+4,t28⟩+C
e
⟨t4+2t,t24⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise, ∫(4t³+2) dt = t⁴+2t and ∫(t/4) dt = t²/8. Thus option b gives the required antiderivative plus an arbitrary constant vector.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨4{t}^{3}+2,\,\frac{t}{4}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨4{t}^{3}+2,\,\frac{t}{4}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (4{t}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{t}{4}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 4
?

If F′(t)=⟨4t3+2,t4⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t2−4t,t8⟩+C
b
⟨t4+2t,t28⟩+C
c
⟨2t4+2,t8⟩+C
d
⟨t+4,t28⟩+C
e
⟨t4+2t,t24⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨4t3+2,t4⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨4t3+2,t4⟩dt=⟨∫(4t3+2)dt,∫t4dt⟩=⟨t4+2t+c1,t28+c2⟩=⟨t4+2t,t28⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨t4+2t,t28⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. Differentiating t⁴+2t gives 4t³+2, and differentiating t²/8 gives t/4. Option a instead has derivative ⟨2t−4, 1/8⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨4{t}^{3}+2,\,\frac{t}{4}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨4{t}^{3}+2,\,\frac{t}{4}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (4{t}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{t}{4}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+2t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ∫sec²(t) dt = tan(t) and ∫−sin(t) dt = cos(t). Therefore option c is the required antiderivative plus a constant vector.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{sec}^{2}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{sec}^{2}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨sec2⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨sec2⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫sec2⁡tdt,∫(−sin⁡t)dt⟩=⟨tan⁡t+c1,cos⁡t+c2⟩=⟨tan⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨tan⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 6
?

Find ∫⟨3t,5t2⟩dt.

a
−⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
b
⟨ln⁡|t|,1t⟩+C
c
⟨ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
d
⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
e
⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate each component: ∫3/t dt = 3ln|t| and ∫5t⁻² dt = −5/t, for t ≠ 0. Adding an arbitrary constant vector gives option e.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{3}{t},\,\frac{5}{{t}^{2}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{3}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{5}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{5}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Find ∫⟨3t,5t2⟩dt.

a
−⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
b
⟨ln⁡|t|,1t⟩+C
c
⟨ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
d
⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
e
⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨3t,5t2⟩dt=⟨∫3tdt,∫5t2dt⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|+c1,−5t+c2⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{3}{t},\,\frac{5}{{t}^{2}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{3}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{5}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{5}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Find ∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt.

a
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t)⟩+C
b
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
c
⟨et−1,sin⁡(t−π6)⟩+C
d
⟨et−1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
e
⟨e5t,5cos⁡(t−π2)⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: ∫eᵗ dt = eᵗ, and ∫10cos(2t−π/6) dt = 5sin(2t−π/6), since the inner derivative is 2. Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =5(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Find ∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt.

a
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t)⟩+C
b
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
c
⟨et−1,sin⁡(t−π6)⟩+C
d
⟨et−1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
e
⟨e5t,5cos⁡(t−π2)⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt=⟨∫etdt,∫10cos⁡(2t−π6)dt⟩.

  • For x(t)=et, we have ∫x(t)dt=∫etdt=et+c1.

  • For y(t)=10cos⁡(2t−π6), we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let u=2t−π6. Then
    dudt=2⟹dt=12du. Therefore, we have ∫y(t)dt=∫10cos⁡(2t−π6)dt=∫10cos⁡u⋅12du=102∫cos⁡udu=5(sin⁡u)+c2=5sin⁡(2t−π6)+c2.

Finally, we get

∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt=⟨et+c1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)+c2⟩=⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. Its derivative is ⟨eᵗ, 10cos(2t−π/6)⟩ by the chain rule. Option a loses the phase shift and instead differentiates to ⟨eᵗ, 10cos(2t)⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =5(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Find ∫⟨cos⁡t,3e(2t+1)⟩dt.

a
⟨sin⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C
b
⟨cos⁡t,e(2t+1)⟩+C
c
⟨sin⁡t,e2t⟩+C
d
⟨cos⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C
e
⟨sin⁡t,(e2t+e)2⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives sin(t) and (3/2)e^{2t+1}. The factor 1/2 compensates for the derivative of 2t+1. Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Find ∫⟨cos⁡t,3e(2t+1)⟩dt.

a
⟨sin⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C
b
⟨cos⁡t,e(2t+1)⟩+C
c
⟨sin⁡t,e2t⟩+C
d
⟨cos⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C
e
⟨sin⁡t,(e2t+e)2⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨cos⁡t,2e(2t+1)⟩dt=⟨∫cos⁡tdt,∫2e(2t+1)dt⟩.

  • For x(t)=cos⁡t, we have ∫x(t)dt=∫cos⁡tdt=sin⁡t+c1.
  • For y(t)=2e(2t+1), we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let u=2t+1. Then
    dudt=2⟹dt=12du. Therefore, we have ∫y(t)dt=∫2e(2t+1)dt=∫3eu⋅12du=32∫eudu=32eu+c2=3e(2t+1)2+c2.

Finally, we get

∫⟨cos⁡t,3e(2t+1)⟩dt=⟨sin⁡t+c1,3e(2t+1)2+c2⟩=⟨sin⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨sin⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

b

decision.explanation: Integrating each component gives ∫eᵗ dt = eᵗ and ∫cos(t) dt = sin(t). Adding an arbitrary constant vector gives option c.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Find ∫⟨1t2,−2t3⟩dt.

a
⟨1t,1t2⟩+C
b
⟨1t,−2t2⟩+C
c
⟨−1t,1t2⟩+C
d
⟨1t2,−2t3⟩+C
e
⟨−1t,t2⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise using the power rule gives ∫t⁻² dt = −1/t and ∫−2t⁻³ dt = 1/t², for t ≠ 0. Thus option c is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -\frac{2}{{t}^{3}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

b
⟨1t,−2t2⟩+C

EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨1t2,1t3⟩dt=⟨∫1t2dt,∫−2t3dt⟩=⟨−1t+c1,1t2+c2⟩=⟨−1t,1t2⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨−1t,1t2⟩+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -\frac{2}{{t}^{3}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (4{t}^{3}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{4}-t+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,1⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨{((1)-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{4}-(1)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+1,\,{t}^{4}-t+1⟩.
$$

\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (4{t}^{3}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{4}-t+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,1⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨{((1)-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{4}-(1)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+1,\,{t}^{4}-t+1⟩.
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating gives ⟨ln|t|+c₁, −cos(πt)+c₂⟩. At t=1, ln(1)=0 and cos(π)=−1, so c₁=−1 and c₂=1. This gives option a.

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨-1,\,2⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-1,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

Question 18
?

If F′(t)=⟨1t,πsin⁡(πt)⟩ and F(1)=⟨−1,2⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨ln⁡|t|−1,1−cos⁡(πt)⟩
b
⟨−1t2+1,cos⁡(πt)+2⟩
c
⟨ln⁡|1−t|,−cos⁡(πt)+2⟩
d
⟨ln⁡|t|−1,−sin⁡(πt)+2⟩
e
⟨ln⁡|t|+1,1−cos⁡(πt)⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨1t,πsin⁡(πt)⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨1t,πsin⁡(πt)⟩dt=⟨∫1tdt,∫πsin⁡(πt)dt⟩=⟨ln⁡|t|+c1,−cos⁡(πt)+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(1)=⟨−1,2⟩ gives F(1)=⟨ln⁡|1|+c1,−cos⁡(π)+c2⟩=⟨−1,2⟩⟨c1,1+c2⟩=⟨−1,2⟩.

Therefore, c1=−1 and c2=1. Consequently F(t)=⟨ln⁡|t|−1,1−cos⁡(πt)⟩.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. Its derivative is ⟨1/t, πsin(πt)⟩, and evaluating at t=1 gives ⟨−1, 2⟩. Option b fails both requirements.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨-1,\,2⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-1,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

Question 19
?

If F′(t)=⟨16t33,5e5t⟩ and F(0)=⟨2,−1⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨4t4/3−2,e5t−2⟩
b
⟨4t1/3+1,et−1⟩
c
⟨4t4/3+2,e5t−2⟩
d
⟨t4/3+2,e2t−5⟩
e
⟨4t4/3+2,5e5t−1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives ⟨4t^{4/3}+c₁, e^{5t}+c₂⟩. The condition F(0)=⟨2,−1⟩ requires c₁=2 and c₂=−2, giving option c.

after.name: Question 19
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 5{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(0)=⟨2,\,-1⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨4\cdot {0}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5\cdot 0}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=-2.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨4{t}^{4/3}+2,\,{e}^{5t}-2⟩.
$$

Question 19

If F′(t)=⟨16t33,5e5t⟩ and F(0)=⟨2,−1⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨4t4/3−2,e5t−2⟩
b
⟨4t1/3+1,et−1⟩
c
⟨4t4/3+2,e5t−2⟩
d
⟨t4/3+2,e2t−5⟩
e
⟨4t4/3+2,5e5t−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨16t33,5e5t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨16t33,5e5t⟩dt=⟨∫16t33dt,∫5e5tdt⟩=⟨4t4/3+c1,e5t+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(0)=⟨2,−1⟩ gives

F(0)=⟨4⋅04/3+c1,e5⋅0+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩⟨c1,1+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩.

Therefore, c1=2 and c2=−2. Consequently F(t)=⟨4t4/3+2,e5t−2⟩.

content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 5{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(0)=⟨2,\,-1⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨4\cdot {0}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5\cdot 0}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=-2.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨4{t}^{4/3}+2,\,{e}^{5t}-2⟩.
$$
